source_text:
On Friday, Maya arranged twenty seedlings beside the school gate. She hoped to sell them to buy replacement hand tools for the garden club. She wrote “Seedlings $2” on a small sign and placed it flat on the table. By lunchtime, eighteen pots remained. Families hurried past, and several glanced towards the table without stopping.

Leo stopped beside her. “I thought these were waiting to be planted,” he said. Maya looked down at the sign, hidden behind the front row of pots. She propped it against a box and added “School garden fundraiser”. For the next few minutes, nobody stopped.

Then a gust knocked two pots sideways. Maya moved the stall into the sheltered entrance. Leo carried the box. As people slowed to open the door, they read the raised sign. One parent bought three seedlings; another asked what the money would buy.

At home time, Maya counted six remaining pots. She put a note in the garden club book: “Next time: entrance, upright sign, explain our purpose.” She left a space underneath for the other members' suggestions.
teacher_think_aloud: At first, I wondered whether families simply did not want seedlings. But the opening only says they hurried past; it doesn't tell me what they wanted. Leo's comment and the hidden sign make me reconsider: perhaps some people didn't realise this was a sale. Maya raises the sign and explains the fundraiser, but nobody stops straight away. Later, in the entrance, people slow down and read it. I think visibility and the location may both have helped. The story doesn't let me prove that one change caused all the extra sales.
